title: SQL Day 9 — Subqueries, EXISTS & Layered Business Analysis
description: Use nested queries to answer questions that depend on another result set or business population.

topics.title: Subquery Fundamentals
topics.business_skill: Use a query result as an input to another query.

teaching.teacher: ## Subqueries\nA subquery is a query nested inside another statement and can provide a value or set of rows to the outer query.
teaching.explain: Use subqueries when the business rule depends on a separately calculated population.
teaching.detailedlearning: Keep inner queries focused and make the outer query express the final business request.
teaching.expose: Nested SQL should have a clear reason; do not add subqueries when a simpler query is sufficient.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders WHERE sales > (SELECT AVG(sales) FROM orders);
teaching.business_question: The manager wants orders above the overall average sales value.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders WHERE sales > (SELECT AVG(sales) FROM orders);

questions.scenario: Finance wants orders above average profit.

questions.scenario: The team wants orders above the average sales of their market.
questions.request: Use a subquery-based approach to compare an order with a market-level average.
questions.validation: Correlated or layered subquery by market

topics.title: Scalar Subqueries
topics.business_skill: Use one calculated value as a business threshold.

teaching.teacher: ## Scalar subquery\nA scalar subquery returns one value, such as an overall average, maximum, or total.
teaching.explain: The outer query can compare each row to that single calculated benchmark.
teaching.detailedlearning: Ensure the subquery returns exactly one value when scalar context requires it.
teaching.expose: If the inner query returns multiple rows, scalar comparison will fail.
teaching.business_question: The director defines high-value orders relative to the overall average.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders WHERE sales > (SELECT AVG(sales) FROM orders);

topics.title: IN & NOT IN
topics.business_skill: Filter rows based on membership in another result set.

teaching.teacher: ## IN\nIN compares a value against a set returned by a subquery. NOT IN excludes members, but NULLs require care.
teaching.explain: Use IN when the business population is defined by another query.
teaching.detailedlearning: Prefer NOT EXISTS when NULL behavior could make NOT IN misleading.
teaching.expose: Membership logic is about set comparison, not text matching.
teaching.example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE segment='Corporate');
teaching.business_question: The sales manager wants orders belonging to Corporate customers.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.sales FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE segment='Corporate');

topics.title: EXISTS & NOT EXISTS
topics.business_skill: Test whether related records exist without needing to return them.

teaching.teacher: ## EXISTS\nEXISTS returns true when the correlated subquery finds at least one related row.
teaching.explain: It is useful for relationship-based business rules such as customers who have orders.
teaching.detailedlearning: Correlate the inner query to the outer row using a key.
teaching.expose: EXISTS asks 'does at least one related record exist?', not 'how many?'.
teaching.example: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id);
teaching.business_question: Customer management wants customers who have placed at least one order.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id);

topics.title: Layered Subquery Analysis
topics.business_skill: Combine subqueries, joins, and aggregation for multi-step business questions.

teaching.teacher: ## Layered analysis\nBreak a complex request into population, metric, and final comparison layers.
teaching.explain: One layer can define a benchmark while another returns the business result.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use subqueries when the intermediate result is conceptually a separate business calculation.
teaching.expose: Complexity becomes manageable when each layer has one responsibility.
teaching.example: SELECT region,total_sales FROM (SELECT region,SUM(sales) total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) x WHERE total_sales > (SELECT AVG(total_sales) FROM (SELECT region,SUM(sales) total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region) y);
teaching.business_question: The director wants regions whose sales are above the average regional sales.
teaching.expected_sql: Use a derived regional-sales table, calculate its average, and filter regions above that benchmark.

questions.request: Return regions whose total sales exceed the average regional total.

questions.request: Return categories whose total profit exceeds the average category profit.
